paragraphs.text: Lesson 15, Talking About the Weather
Welcome to Lesson 15 of the Everyday English Speaking Course.
In this lesson, you'll learn practical words and phrases for describing the current weather
and temperature, as well as predicting weather conditions in the future.
Conversation number 1, Summer Weather
Brad and Carol are neighbors living in South Carolina.
Listen to this conversation during one day in June.
It's a beautiful day, isn't it?
Sure is.
There's not a cloud in the sky.
And it's not too hot or humid either.
I love it when it's warm with a light breeze.
Yeah, it's supposed to be a real scorcher tomorrow, though.
Oh, really?
That's perfect, because my kids have a pool party in the afternoon.
I wonder if we're going to have a heat wave like last summer.
I don't think so.
They say we're going to get some thunderstorms over the weekend, so the rain should cool things
off.
That's good.
Well, I'm off to the park.
I'll catch you later.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
To start, Carol says, it's a beautiful day, isn't it?
This is a common way to begin a casual conversation.
Here are some additional phrases for asking about the weather.
How's the weather?
What's the weather like today?
It's a beautiful day, isn't it?
Terrible weather, isn't it?
These two questions ending in, isn't it, are ways to initiate a conversation, because the
other person will agree with your comment.
What's the weather forecast?
The forecast means the prediction of the weather in the future.
What's the temperature?
Is it hot out?
Or is it cold out?
The most basic way to describe current weather conditions are these phrases.
It's sunny.
It's cloudy.
It's cloudy.
It's rainy.
It's foggy.
It's windy.
It's humid.
And to describe the temperature, you can say, it's boiling.
It's hot.
It's warm.
It's mild.
It's cool.
It's chilly.
It's cold.
It's freezing.
It's about 70 degrees.
You can also describe the weather more generally with these typical adjectives.
For good weather, you can say, the weather's great, fantastic, gorgeous, or perfect.
And for bad weather, you can say, the weather's terrible, lousy, or awful.
Here are a few common phrases for talking about hot and sunny weather.
The sun is shining.
It sure is a scorcher today.
A scorcher is a very hot day.
There isn't a cloud in the sky.
We're having a real heat wave.
A heat wave is a series of hot days.
I got a bad sunburn.
A sunburn is when your skin turns red and hurts because of too much sun.
Make sure to use sunscreen.
Sunscreen protects your skin from a sunburn.
I'm all sweaty.
It's unbearably hot.
This means it's extremely hot in a negative sense and you are uncomfortable.
Conversation number two, winter weather.
Lindsey in New York calls her cousin Joe who's on vacation in Florida in the month of January.
Hey Joe, how's the weather in Florida?
Terrible.
We've had really heavy rain.
It's pouring right now.
Ah, well, at least it's warm.
It's freezing here in New York and we're expecting a blizzard tomorrow.
Eh, I couldn't call it warm.
It's mild, but when the wind picks up it can get pretty chilly.
That's too bad.
I hope it clears up and the sun comes out so you can enjoy your vacation.
Yeah, the forecast is the rain will let up by tomorrow morning.
So how much snow are you expecting?
They say we're going to get six to eight inches.
I have a feeling school will be canceled.
Right, we'll make sure you bundle up and drive carefully on those icy roads.
I will.
Alright Joe, I've got to get ready for class.
Enjoy the rest of your trip.
Thanks Lindsey.
Talk to you later.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
In this dialogue we hear various phrases about rainy, cloudy, windy and snowy weather.
Let's learn some phrases for talking about rain.
It looks like rain.
This means it is not yet raining, but it appears that it will rain soon.
It's drizzling.
Drizzling means raining lightly.
It's pouring.
Pouring means raining heavily.
I got caught in the rain.
This means you were outside when it started to rain.
I hope the rain lets up.
This means you hope the rain stops.
We had a downpour.
A downpour is a sudden period of heavy rain.
We had a thunderstorm.
A thunderstorm is heavy rain with thunder and lightning.
The heavy rain is causing flooding.
Flooding means that there's too much water causing damage to land and buildings.
Here are some phrases for talking about snow.
It's snowing.
We're having a snowstorm or blizzard.
We're expecting six to eight inches.
The roads are icy or slippery.
I slipped on the ice while walking to school.
When walking, the verb to use is slipped.
My car skidded on the icy road.
When driving, the verb to use is skidded.
Here are some phrases for talking about clouds.
It's gloomy.
This means the day is dark and depressing because clouds are blocking the sun.
It's foggy.
It's overcast.
Overcast means the sky is completely covered with clouds.
It's clearing up.
This means the clouds are starting to go away.
The sun is coming out.
This means the sun is starting to appear.
Here are some typical phrases for talking about wind.
There's a light breeze.
This phrase describes a weak and pleasant wind.
The wind's picking up.
The wind's dying down.
Picking up means getting stronger and dying down means getting weaker.
The wind is blowing.
There are gale force winds.
Gale force winds are extremely strong winds.
A gust of wind almost knocked me over.
Finally, in both conversations there are phrases describing the prediction of the weather in
the future.
We call this prediction the weather forecast and there are a number of different ways to
express it in English.
The forecast says it's going to rain tomorrow.
The forecast says we're going to get 6 inches of snow.
The forecast says it will be sunny this weekend.
It's supposed to get a little warmer tomorrow.
It's supposed to clear up by the evening.
It's supposed to be hot and humid all week.
They say there will be a thunderstorm this afternoon.
They say it will be chilly tomorrow.
They say we're going to have a heat wave.
We're expecting hot, cold, humid, mild, warm or chilly weather.
We're expecting rain, snow, a thunderstorm or a blizzard.
There's a 90% chance of rain, snow or thunderstorms.
So now you know a lot of different ways to describe the weather.
Today's speaking challenge is to leave a message talking about the current weather
and temperature where you are and the weather forecast in your area.
If you don't know the forecast, look it up online.
Click on the link in the lesson text to record a message.
Don't be shy.
